p.x:
Last year, my grandmother got her first smartphone. At first, she didn't like it. The screen was too small, and she couldn't remember her password. She also forgot to charge the battery, so it was often dead.
Now she loves it! Every morning, she sends messages to her friends and reads the news on the internet. Her favourite app is a video app where she watches cooking videos. She also takes photos of her garden and sends them to the family group. Last week she called me on a video call for the first time. "It's like you're in my kitchen!" she said. Now she wants a computer too.

p.t: Five Ways to Protect Your Devices
p.x:
Our phones and laptops contain more personal information than ever. Here are five simple ways to protect them.
1. Update your software. Updates often fix security problems, so install them as soon as they are available, even if it takes a few minutes.
2. Use strong passwords. A good password is long and includes numbers and symbols. Never use the same password for every website.
3. Be careful with attachments. If you receive an email from someone you don't know, don't open the attachment. Just delete it.
4. Avoid public wireless networks for banking. Free Wi-Fi in cafés is convenient, but other users on the same network may be able to see what you are doing.
5. Back up your files. If your device crashes, is stolen, or you spill coffee on the keyboard, you won't lose everything. Upload important photos and documents to the cloud once a week, or copy them to an external drive.

Have you ever picked up your phone to check the time and found yourself still scrolling twenty minutes later? That is not an accident. Many apps are deliberately designed to be addictive. Every notification, like and new video gives the brain a small reward, and an algorithm learns exactly which content will keep each user watching for longer.
Technology companies argue that this is simply good design: people use their products because they enjoy them. Critics, however, point to rising rates of anxiety among teenagers and to the spread of cyberbullying, which follows young people home from school. Privacy is another concern. The more time we spend online, the more personal data companies can collect and sell to advertisers. Although many messaging apps now use encryption, our browsing habits are rarely so well protected.
Not all innovation is harmful, of course. The same smartphones that distract us also allow doctors to monitor patients remotely and farmers to check weather forecasts. And the constant pressure to upgrade, which makes perfectly good gadgets seem obsolete after two or three years, is partly driven by consumers themselves. Perhaps the real question is not whether technology is good or bad, but whether we control it or it controls us.
